Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 113, verses 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata', and Jabir, and Medinan according to one of the two opinions attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and to Qatadah. Ahmad, al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted through several chains, which al-Suyuti called sound, that Ibn Mas'ud used to scratch out the two Mu'awwidhatayn (the two surahs of seeking refuge, 113 and 114) from the mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), saying: "Do not mix the Qur'an with what is not part of it. They are not from the Book of Allah. The Prophet (ﷺ) was only commanded to seek refuge with them." And Ibn Mas'ud would not recite them.

Al-Bazzar said: No one among the Companions followed Ibn Mas'ud in this. It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited them in prayer, and they were affirmed in the mushaf.

Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, and others transmitted from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: "I came to Medina and met Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and I said to him: 'O Abu al-Mundhir, I have seen that Ibn Mas'ud does not write the two Mu'awwidhatayn in his mushaf.' He said: 'By Him who sent Muhammad with the truth, I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about them, and no one has asked me about them since I asked him except you. He said: It was said to me: Say. So I said it. So we say what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said.'"

Al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about these two surahs, and he said: "It was said to me, so I said. So say what I said."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others transmitted from Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tonight there were revealed to me verses the like of which I have never seen: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾."

Ibn al-Dhurays, Ibn al-Anbari, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh in al-Shu'ab transmitted from Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, teach me Surah Yusuf and Surah Hud.' He said: 'O Uqbah, recite ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, for you will never recite a surah more beloved to Allah or more effective than it. If you can avoid missing it, then do so.'"

Ibn Sa'd, al-Nasa'i, al-Baghawi, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Habis al-Juhani that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Habis, shall I inform you of the best of what those who seek refuge seek refuge with?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾; they are the two Mu'awwidhatayn.

Al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to seek refuge from the evil eye of the jinn and the evil eye of humans. When the two Mu'awwidhatayn were revealed, he took them and left what was other than them."

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, and al-Hakim (who graded it sound) transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked ten things, and among them that he disliked incantations (ruqa) except with the two Mu'awwidhatayn.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Umm Salamah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Among the surahs most beloved to Allah are ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾."

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Dhurays, Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took me by the shoulder and said: 'Recite.' I said: 'What should I recite, may my father and mother be your ransom?' He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. Then he said: 'Recite.' I said: 'May my father and mother be your ransom, what should I recite?' He said: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾, and you have not recited the like of these two."

Malik in the Muwatta' transmitted from Ibn Shihab, from 'Urwah, from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite over himself with the two Mu'awwidhatayn when he was ill, and would blow (nafth). When his pain intensified, I would recite over him and wipe his hand over him, seeking the blessing of them.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their Sahihs also transmitted it through the chain of Malik as mentioned.

'Abd ibn Humayd in his Musnad transmitted from Zayd ibn Arqam, who said: "A man from the Jews cast a spell on the Prophet (ﷺ), and he fell ill. Jibril came to him and descended upon him with the two Mu'awwidhatayn, and said: 'A man from the Jews has cast a spell on you, and the magic is in the well of so-and-so.' He sent 'Ali, who came with it, and he commanded him to untie the knots, reciting a verse and untying, until the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up as if he had been released from a fetter."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi also transmitted it from the hadith of 'A'ishah at length, and Ibn Mardawayh likewise transmitted it from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas.

Traditions have come concerning the virtue of the two Mu'awwidhatayn, and concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) reciting them in prayer and otherwise. What we have mentioned is sufficient.

Al-Tabarani in al-Saghir transmitted from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: "A scorpion stung the Prophet (ﷺ) while he was praying. When he finished he said: 'May Allah curse the scorpion, it spares neither one who prays nor anyone else.' Then he asked for water and salt, and began wiping over the sting while reciting: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾, ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾."

Al-falaq is the dawn (al-subh). It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn." It was named falaq because the night is split away from it (yuflaqu 'anhu al-layl). It is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive). Al-Zajjaj said: Because the dawn splits forth from the night (yanfaliqu 'anhu al-subh), and it is in the sense of maf'ul. It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn, and than the faraq of the dawn." This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Until, when the falaq withdrew from its face, calm, at the latter part of the night, rising up.

And the saying of another:

O night which I did not sleep through, I spent it propped up, watching the stars until the falaq brightened.

It has also been said that al-falaq is a prison in Hell. It has been said it is one of the names of Hell. It has been said it is a tree in the Fire. It has been said it is the mountains and the rocks, because they are split by water, i.e., cracked. It has been said it is the splitting between mountains, because they split out of fear of Allah.

Al-Nahhas said: Every low-lying piece of land is called falaq. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

I kept watching them until, when the hands of the riders brought them down, from Raki' falaqa.

Al-Raki' is the bottom of the valley.

Similar is the saying of al-Nabigha:

And behind me is Raki', then the Dawajih.

It has been said it is the womb, which splits open with the living being. It has been said it is everything that splits open to bring forth all that Allah created of living beings, of the dawn, of grain and date-pits, and of every plant and other thing. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Al-Qurtubi said: This view is supported by the splitting (al-infiqaq), for al-falq is the cleaving (al-shaqq). One says falaqtu al-shay' falqan: I cleaved it. The taflIq is similar to it. It is said falaqtuhu fa-nfalaqa and tafallaqa. So everything that splits open from something, of living beings, dawn, grain, date-pits, or water, is falaq. End of quote.

Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and He said: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-pit﴾ [al-An'am: 95]. End.

The first opinion is more preferable, because although the meaning of the other is more general and broader than what the first includes, the first is what comes to mind upon an unrestricted reading.

It has been said regarding the specification of al-falaq that it alludes to the fact that the One who is able to remove these intense darknesses from this entire world is also able to repel from the one seeking refuge everything he fears and dreads. It has also been said that the rising of dawn is like an example of the coming of relief. Just as a person in the night awaits the morning, so the fearful one awaits the dawn of success. It has been said other than this, which is merely an explanation of a relationship with little benefit related to the exegesis.

﴿From the evil of what He created﴾ is connected to a'udhu (I seek refuge). That is: from the evil of everything He created, of all His creatures; so it encompasses all evils. It has been said it is Iblis and his offspring; it has been said it is Hell. There is no basis for this specification, just as there is no basis for those who specify this generality as referring to bodily harms.

Some zealous partisans distorted this verse in defense of their school and in support of their falsehood. They read "sharrin" with tanwin, taking "ma" as a negation, and the meaning becomes: "from an evil He did not create." Among them were 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and 'Amr ibn 'A'idh.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Al-ghasiq is the night, and al-ghasaq is darkness. One says ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu, when it became dark.

Al-Farra' said: It is said ghasaqa al-layl and aghsaqa when it became dark. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Raqiyat:

Indeed this night has grown dark, and I complained of worry and sleeplessness.

Al-Zajjaj said: The night is called ghasiq because it is colder than the day, and al-ghasiq is the cold, and al-ghasaq is coldness. And because in the night beasts of prey come out of their thickets, and venomous creatures out of their places, and the people of evil rise up to mischief and corruption. Thus he said, and it is a weak opinion, for the people of language are against it, as is the majority of exegetes.

Its waqub is the entry of its darkness. From it is the saying of the poet:

The punishment settled upon them, so they became as if the scorching wind's fire had reached them and they were extinguished.

That is: punishment entered upon them. It is said: waqabat al-shams, when the sun set. It has been said al-ghasiq is the Pleiades, because when it sets diseases and plagues increase, and when it rises that is lifted. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

This needs transmission from the Arabs that they describe the Pleiades with ghusuq.

Al-Zuhri said: It is the sun when it sets, and it seems he considered the meaning of waqub and did not consider the meaning of ghusuq. It has been said it is the moon when it eclipses, and it has been said when it sets.

With this Qatadah and others said, and they cited a hadith transmitted by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh, from 'A'ishah, who said: "One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the moon when it rose and said: 'O 'A'ishah, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it waqab.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: It is hasan sahih. This does not contradict the view of the majority, because the moon is a sign of the night and it has no authority except within it. The same is said in response to the one who said it is the Pleiades.

Ibn al-A'rabi said in explaining this hadith: That is because the people of doubt watch for the moment of the moon's eclipse (wajbat al-qamar).

It has been said al-ghasiq is the snake when it stings.

It has been said al-ghasiq is every attacker that harms, whatever it may be, from the saying: ghasaqat al-quhrah, when its pus flowed.

It has been said al-ghasiq is the one who asks (al-sa'il). We have made clear to you that the preferred interpretation of this verse is what the people of the first view said, and the reason for specifying it is that evil in it is greater, and guarding against evils in it is more difficult. From it is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the wicked (al-layl akhfa lil-wayl)."

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Al-naffathat are the female sorcerers, that is: and from the evil of the blowing souls, or the blowing women. Al-nafth is blowing, as those who perform incantations and sorcery do. It is said it is with saliva, and it is said without saliva. Al-'uqad is the plural of 'uqdah. That is because they used to blow into the knots of threads when they cast spells with them. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

If he recovers, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then the losing is his due.

And the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

He blew into the thread, like incantations, out of fear of the jinn and the envier.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: The naffathat are the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, who cast spells on the Prophet (ﷺ).

The majority read al-naffathat, the plural of naffathah, in intensive form.

Ya'qub, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read al-nafithat, the plural of nafithah.

al-Hasan read al-nuffathat with a damma on the nun.

Abu al-Rabi' read al-nafathat without an alif.

﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. Hasad (envy) is wishing for the removal of the blessing which Allah has bestowed upon the one envied. The meaning of "when he envies" is: when he manifests what is in his soul of envy, acts upon its demands, and envy drives him to inflict harm upon the envied.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: I have not seen a wrongdoer more like the wronged than the envier. The poet has versified this meaning, saying:

Say to the envier when he breathes out a thrust: "O wrongdoer," while he seems to be the wronged one.

In this surah, Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the instruction to His Messenger (ﷺ) to seek refuge from the evil of all His creatures in general. Then He mentioned some evils in particular, although they fall under the generality, to increase the emphasis on their evil and the greatness of their harm: they are the ghasiq, the naffathat, and the envier. So it is as if these, because of the greater evil in them, deserve to be mentioned individually.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 113, verses 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Amr ibn Abasa, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer and recited ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. Then he said: 'O son of Abasa, do you know what al-Falaq (the daybreak) is?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a well in Hell.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it as the words of Amr ibn Abasa, not as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet) report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Uqba ibn Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Recite ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. Do you know what al-Falaq is? It is a gate in the Fire; when it is opened, Hell is kindled.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. He said: 'It is a prison in Hell, in which the tyrants and the arrogant are confined, and Hell itself seeks refuge in Allah from it.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "al-Falaq is a pit in Hell."

These hadiths, if they were authentic and established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it would be obligatory to turn to them and necessary to adopt their view.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Falaq is a prison in Hell."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "al-Falaq is the dawn."

Ibn Jarir narrated the like of this from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "al-Falaq is the creation."

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning his words: ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, that he said: "The star is the ghasiq, and it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from another route from him, not as a marfu' report.

It has already been mentioned the interpretation (ta'wil) of what has been reported, that the ghasiq is the moon.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him also, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the stars rise, every calamity is lifted from every land." Even if this were authentic, it would not be evidence that the ghasiq is the star or the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, that he said: "It is the night when it comes."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾, that he said: "They are the female sorcerers."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "It is what mixes with magic (sihr) of incantations (ruqa)."

al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever ties a knot and then blows into it has practised magic; and whoever practises magic has committed shirk; and whoever hangs something (as an amulet) is left to it."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to visit me and said: 'Shall I not recite a ruqya over you with which Jibril recited over me?' I said: 'Yes, may my father and mother be your ransom.' He said: 'In the name of Allah I recite over you; Allah cures you from every ailment within you, from the evil of the blowers in knots, and from the evil of the envier when he envies.' And he recited it over him three times."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning his words: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾, that he said: "It is the soul (nafs) and the eye of the son of Adam." (End.)

Al-Tabarani transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud that the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about these two surahs, and he said: "It was said to me, so I said. So say what I said."

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others transmitted from Uqbah ibn 'Amir, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Tonight there were revealed to me verses the like of which I have never seen: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾ and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾."

He said: 'O Uqbah, recite ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, for you will never recite a surah more beloved to Allah or more effective than it. If you can avoid missing it, then do so.'"

Ibn Sa'd, al-Nasa'i, al-Baghawi, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Abu Habis al-Juhani that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "O Abu Habis, shall I inform you of the best of what those who seek refuge seek refuge with?" In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-falaq is the dawn (al-subh). It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn." It was named falaq because the night is split away from it (yuflaqu 'anhu al-layl). It is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive). Al-Zajjaj said: Because the dawn splits forth from the night (yanfaliqu 'anhu al-subh), and it is in the sense of maf'ul. It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn, and than the faraq of the dawn." This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Until, when the falaq withdrew from its face, calm, at the latter part of the night, rising up.

And the saying of another:

O night which I did not sleep through, I spent it propped up, watching the stars until the falaq brightened.

It has also been said that al-falaq is a prison in Hell. It has been said it is one of the names of Hell. It has been said it is a tree in the Fire. It has been said it is the mountains and the rocks, because they are split by water, i.e., cracked. It has been said it is the splitting between mountains, because they split out of fear of Allah.

Al-Nahhas said: Every low-lying piece of land is called falaq. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

I kept watching them until, when the hands of the riders brought them down, from Raki' falaqa.

Al-Raki' is the bottom of the valley.

Similar is the saying of al-Nabigha:

And behind me is Raki', then the Dawajih.

It has been said it is the womb, which splits open with the living being. It has been said it is everything that splits open to bring forth all that Allah created of living beings, of the dawn, of grain and date-pits, and of every plant and other thing. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Al-Qurtubi said: This view is supported by the splitting (al-infiqaq), for al-falq is the cleaving (al-shaqq). One says falaqtu al-shay' falqan: I cleaved it. The taflIq is similar to it. It is said falaqtuhu fa-nfalaqa and tafallaqa. So everything that splits open from something, of living beings, dawn, grain, date-pits, or water, is falaq. End of quote.

Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and He said: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-pit﴾ [al-An'am: 95]. End.

The first opinion is more preferable, because although the meaning of the other is more general and broader than what the first includes, the first is what comes to mind upon an unrestricted reading.

It has been said regarding the specification of al-falaq that it alludes to the fact that the One who is able to remove these intense darknesses from this entire world is also able to repel from the one seeking refuge everything he fears and dreads. It has also been said that the rising of dawn is like an example of the coming of relief. Just as a person in the night awaits the morning, so the fearful one awaits the dawn of success. It has been said other than this, which is merely an explanation of a relationship with little benefit related to the exegesis.

﴿From the evil of what He created﴾ is connected to a'udhu (I seek refuge). That is: from the evil of everything He created, of all His creatures; so it encompasses all evils. It has been said it is Iblis and his offspring; it has been said it is Hell. There is no basis for this specification, just as there is no basis for those who specify this generality as referring to bodily harms.

Some zealous partisans distorted this verse in defense of their school and in support of their falsehood. They read "sharrin" with tanwin, taking "ma" as a negation, and the meaning becomes: "from an evil He did not create." Among them were 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and 'Amr ibn 'A'idh.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Al-ghasiq is the night, and al-ghasaq is darkness. One says ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu, when it became dark.

Al-Farra' said: It is said ghasaqa al-layl and aghsaqa when it became dark. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Raqiyat:

Indeed this night has grown dark, and I complained of worry and sleeplessness.

Al-Zajjaj said: The night is called ghasiq because it is colder than the day, and al-ghasiq is the cold, and al-ghasaq is coldness. And because in the night beasts of prey come out of their thickets, and venomous creatures out of their places, and the people of evil rise up to mischief and corruption. Thus he said, and it is a weak opinion, for the people of language are against it, as is the majority of exegetes.

Its waqub is the entry of its darkness. From it is the saying of the poet:

The punishment settled upon them, so they became as if the scorching wind's fire had reached them and they were extinguished.

That is: punishment entered upon them. It is said: waqabat al-shams, when the sun set. It has been said al-ghasiq is the Pleiades, because when it sets diseases and plagues increase, and when it rises that is lifted. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

This needs transmission from the Arabs that they describe the Pleiades with ghusuq.

Al-Zuhri said: It is the sun when it sets, and it seems he considered the meaning of waqub and did not consider the meaning of ghusuq. It has been said it is the moon when it eclipses, and it has been said when it sets.

With this Qatadah and others said, and they cited a hadith transmitted by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh, from 'A'ishah, who said: "One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the moon when it rose and said: 'O 'A'ishah, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it waqab.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: It is hasan sahih. This does not contradict the view of the majority, because the moon is a sign of the night and it has no authority except within it. The same is said in response to the one who said it is the Pleiades.

Ibn al-A'rabi said in explaining this hadith: That is because the people of doubt watch for the moment of the moon's eclipse (wajbat al-qamar).

It has been said al-ghasiq is the snake when it stings.

It has been said al-ghasiq is every attacker that harms, whatever it may be, from the saying: ghasaqat al-quhrah, when its pus flowed.

It has been said al-ghasiq is the one who asks (al-sa'il). We have made clear to you that the preferred interpretation of this verse is what the people of the first view said, and the reason for specifying it is that evil in it is greater, and guarding against evils in it is more difficult. From it is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the wicked (al-layl akhfa lil-wayl)."

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Al-naffathat are the female sorcerers, that is: and from the evil of the blowing souls, or the blowing women. Al-nafth is blowing, as those who perform incantations and sorcery do. It is said it is with saliva, and it is said without saliva. Al-'uqad is the plural of 'uqdah. That is because they used to blow into the knots of threads when they cast spells with them. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

If he recovers, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then the losing is his due.

And the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

He blew into the thread, like incantations, out of fear of the jinn and the envier.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: The naffathat are the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, who cast spells on the Prophet (ﷺ).

The majority read al-naffathat, the plural of naffathah, in intensive form.

Ya'qub, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read al-nafithat, the plural of nafithah.

al-Hasan read al-nuffathat with a damma on the nun.

Abu al-Rabi' read al-nafathat without an alif.

﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. Hasad (envy) is wishing for the removal of the blessing which Allah has bestowed upon the one envied. The meaning of "when he envies" is: when he manifests what is in his soul of envy, acts upon its demands, and envy drives him to inflict harm upon the envied.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: I have not seen a wrongdoer more like the wronged than the envier. The poet has versified this meaning, saying:

Say to the envier when he breathes out a thrust: "O wrongdoer," while he seems to be the wronged one.

In this surah, Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the instruction to His Messenger (ﷺ) to seek refuge from the evil of all His creatures in general. Then He mentioned some evils in particular, although they fall under the generality, to increase the emphasis on their evil and the greatness of their harm: they are the ghasiq, the naffathat, and the envier. So it is as if these, because of the greater evil in them, deserve to be mentioned individually.

Then he asked for water and salt, and began wiping over the sting while reciting: ﴿Say: O disbelievers﴾, ﴿Say: He is Allah, One﴾, ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾, and ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of mankind﴾."

(p-1670)
In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Al-falaq is the dawn (al-subh). It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn." It was named falaq because the night is split away from it (yuflaqu 'anhu al-layl). It is on the pattern fa'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive). Al-Zajjaj said: Because the dawn splits forth from the night (yanfaliqu 'anhu al-subh), and it is in the sense of maf'ul. It is said: "He is clearer than the falaq of the dawn, and than the faraq of the dawn." This is the view of the majority of the exegetes. From it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Until, when the falaq withdrew from its face, calm, at the latter part of the night, rising up.

And the saying of another:

O night which I did not sleep through, I spent it propped up, watching the stars until the falaq brightened.

It has also been said that al-falaq is a prison in Hell. It has been said it is one of the names of Hell. It has been said it is a tree in the Fire. It has been said it is the mountains and the rocks, because they are split by water, i.e., cracked. It has been said it is the splitting between mountains, because they split out of fear of Allah.

Al-Nahhas said: Every low-lying piece of land is called falaq. From it is the saying of Zuhayr:

I kept watching them until, when the hands of the riders brought them down, from Raki' falaqa.

Al-Raki' is the bottom of the valley.

Similar is the saying of al-Nabigha:

And behind me is Raki', then the Dawajih.

It has been said it is the womb, which splits open with the living being. It has been said it is everything that splits open to bring forth all that Allah created of living beings, of the dawn, of grain and date-pits, and of every plant and other thing. This was said by al-Hasan and al-Dahhak.

Al-Qurtubi said: This view is supported by the splitting (al-infiqaq), for al-falq is the cleaving (al-shaqq). One says falaqtu al-shay' falqan: I cleaved it. The taflIq is similar to it. It is said falaqtuhu fa-nfalaqa and tafallaqa. So everything that splits open from something, of living beings, dawn, grain, date-pits, or water, is falaq. End of quote.

Allah, glorified is He, said: ﴿Splitter of the dawn﴾ [al-An'am: 96], and He said: ﴿Splitter of the grain and the date-pit﴾ [al-An'am: 95]. End.

The first opinion is more preferable, because although the meaning of the other is more general and broader than what the first includes, the first is what comes to mind upon an unrestricted reading.

It has been said regarding the specification of al-falaq that it alludes to the fact that the One who is able to remove these intense darknesses from this entire world is also able to repel from the one seeking refuge everything he fears and dreads. It has also been said that the rising of dawn is like an example of the coming of relief. Just as a person in the night awaits the morning, so the fearful one awaits the dawn of success. It has been said other than this, which is merely an explanation of a relationship with little benefit related to the exegesis.

﴿From the evil of what He created﴾ is connected to a'udhu (I seek refuge). That is: from the evil of everything He created, of all His creatures; so it encompasses all evils. It has been said it is Iblis and his offspring; it has been said it is Hell. There is no basis for this specification, just as there is no basis for those who specify this generality as referring to bodily harms.

Some zealous partisans distorted this verse in defense of their school and in support of their falsehood. They read "sharrin" with tanwin, taking "ma" as a negation, and the meaning becomes: "from an evil He did not create." Among them were 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd and 'Amr ibn 'A'idh.

﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾. Al-ghasiq is the night, and al-ghasaq is darkness. One says ghasaqa al-layl, yaghsiqu, when it became dark.

Al-Farra' said: It is said ghasaqa al-layl and aghsaqa when it became dark. From it is the saying of Qays ibn al-Raqiyat:

Indeed this night has grown dark, and I complained of worry and sleeplessness.

Al-Zajjaj said: The night is called ghasiq because it is colder than the day, and al-ghasiq is the cold, and al-ghasaq is coldness. And because in the night beasts of prey come out of their thickets, and venomous creatures out of their places, and the people of evil rise up to mischief and corruption. Thus he said, and it is a weak opinion, for the people of language are against it, as is the majority of exegetes.

Its waqub is the entry of its darkness. From it is the saying of the poet:

The punishment settled upon them, so they became as if the scorching wind's fire had reached them and they were extinguished.

That is: punishment entered upon them. It is said: waqabat al-shams, when the sun set. It has been said al-ghasiq is the Pleiades, because when it sets diseases and plagues increase, and when it rises that is lifted. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

This needs transmission from the Arabs that they describe the Pleiades with ghusuq.

Al-Zuhri said: It is the sun when it sets, and it seems he considered the meaning of waqub and did not consider the meaning of ghusuq. It has been said it is the moon when it eclipses, and it has been said when it sets.

With this Qatadah and others said, and they cited a hadith transmitted by Ahmad, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, al-Hakim (who graded it sound), and Ibn Mardawayh, from 'A'ishah, who said: "One day the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) looked at the moon when it rose and said: 'O 'A'ishah, seek refuge in Allah from the evil of this, for this is the ghasiq when it waqab.'"

Al-Tirmidhi said after transmitting it: It is hasan sahih. This does not contradict the view of the majority, because the moon is a sign of the night and it has no authority except within it. The same is said in response to the one who said it is the Pleiades.

Ibn al-A'rabi said in explaining this hadith: That is because the people of doubt watch for the moment of the moon's eclipse (wajbat al-qamar).

It has been said al-ghasiq is the snake when it stings.

It has been said al-ghasiq is every attacker that harms, whatever it may be, from the saying: ghasaqat al-quhrah, when its pus flowed.

It has been said al-ghasiq is the one who asks (al-sa'il). We have made clear to you that the preferred interpretation of this verse is what the people of the first view said, and the reason for specifying it is that evil in it is greater, and guarding against evils in it is more difficult. From it is their saying: "The night is more concealing for the wicked (al-layl akhfa lil-wayl)."

﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾. Al-naffathat are the female sorcerers, that is: and from the evil of the blowing souls, or the blowing women. Al-nafth is blowing, as those who perform incantations and sorcery do. It is said it is with saliva, and it is said without saliva. Al-'uqad is the plural of 'uqdah. That is because they used to blow into the knots of threads when they cast spells with them. From it is the saying of 'Antarah:

If he recovers, I did not blow upon him; and if he is lost, then the losing is his due.

And the saying of Mutammim ibn Nuwayrah:

He blew into the thread, like incantations, out of fear of the jinn and the envier.

Abu 'Ubaydah said: The naffathat are the daughters of Labid ibn al-A'sam, the Jew, who cast spells on the Prophet (ﷺ).

The majority read al-naffathat, the plural of naffathah, in intensive form.

Ya'qub, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabat, and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read al-nafithat, the plural of nafithah.

al-Hasan read al-nuffathat with a damma on the nun.

Abu al-Rabi' read al-nafathat without an alif.

﴿And from the evil of an envier when he envies﴾. Hasad (envy) is wishing for the removal of the blessing which Allah has bestowed upon the one envied. The meaning of "when he envies" is: when he manifests what is in his soul of envy, acts upon its demands, and envy drives him to inflict harm upon the envied.

'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said: I have not seen a wrongdoer more like the wronged than the envier. The poet has versified this meaning, saying:

Say to the envier when he breathes out a thrust: "O wrongdoer," while he seems to be the wronged one.

In this surah, Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the instruction to His Messenger (ﷺ) to seek refuge from the evil of all His creatures in general. Then He mentioned some evils in particular, although they fall under the generality, to increase the emphasis on their evil and the greatness of their harm: they are the ghasiq, the naffathat, and the envier. So it is as if these, because of the greater evil in them, deserve to be mentioned individually.

Al-Shawkani, *Fath al-Qadir*, commentary on Surah 113, verses 1–5 (part 2 of 2):

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Amr ibn Abasa, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) led us in prayer and recited ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. Then he said: 'O son of Abasa, do you know what al-Falaq (the daybreak) is?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It is a well in Hell.'"

Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it as the words of Amr ibn Abasa, not as a marfu' (traced directly to the Prophet) report.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Uqba ibn Amir, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to me: 'Recite ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. Do you know what al-Falaq is? It is a gate in the Fire; when it is opened, Hell is kindled.'"

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Daylami narrated from Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As, who said: "I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Say: I seek refuge in the Lord of the daybreak﴾. He said: 'It is a prison in Hell, in which the tyrants and the arrogant are confined, and Hell itself seeks refuge in Allah from it.'"

Ibn Jarir narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "al-Falaq is a pit in Hell."

These hadiths, if they were authentic and established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), it would be obligatory to turn to them and necessary to adopt their view.

Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: "al-Falaq is a prison in Hell."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Jabir ibn Abdullah, who said: "al-Falaq is the dawn."

Ibn Jarir narrated the like of this from Ibn Abbas.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him (Ibn Abbas), who said: "al-Falaq is the creation."

Ibn Jarir, Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning his words: ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, that he said: "The star is the ghasiq, and it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from another route from him, not as a marfu' report.

It has already been mentioned the interpretation (ta'wil) of what has been reported, that the ghasiq is the moon.

Abu al-Shaykh narrated from him also, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When the stars rise, every calamity is lifted from every land." Even if this were authentic, it would not be evidence that the ghasiq is the star or the stars.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And from the evil of the darkness when it settles﴾, that he said: "It is the night when it comes."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning ﴿And from the evil of the blowers in knots﴾, that he said: "They are the female sorcerers."

Ibn Jarir narrated from him concerning the verse, that he said: "It is what mixes with magic (sihr) of incantations (ruqa)."

al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever ties a knot and then blows into it has practised magic; and whoever practises magic has committed shirk; and whoever hangs something (as an amulet) is left to it."

Ibn Sa'd, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayra, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) came to visit me and said: 'Shall I not recite a ruqya over you with which Jibril recited over me?' I said: 'Yes, may my father and mother be your ransom.' He said: 'In the name of Allah I recite over you; Allah cures you from every ailment within you, from the evil of the blowers in knots, and from the evil of the envier when he envies.' And he recited it over him three times."

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas concerning his words: ﴿And from the evil of the envier when he envies﴾, that he said: "It is the soul (nafs) and the eye of the son of Adam." (End.)
